micros.title: Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive Relations
micros.description: Test a relation on a set for reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity from its defining rule or its list of ordered pairs, producing counterexamples where a property fails.
outcomes: Can check each of the three properties for a relation given as pairs or as a rule
Can produce a specific counterexample pair whenever a property fails

micros.title: Equivalence Relations and Equivalence Classes
micros.description: Recognise relations that are reflexive, symmetric and transitive as equivalence relations, and describe the partition of the set into equivalence classes (e.g. congruence modulo n).
outcomes: Can verify that a relation is an equivalence relation
Can list the equivalence classes of relations like 'a ≡ b (mod 3)' and explain why classes partition the set

micros.title: One-one (Injective) Functions
micros.description: Prove a function is one-one by showing f(x1) = f(x2) forces x1 = x2, or disprove it with two distinct inputs sharing an output; read injectivity off a graph with the horizontal line test.
outcomes: Can prove or disprove injectivity algebraically
Can state the difference between 'every input has one output' (function) and 'distinct inputs have distinct outputs' (one-one)

question.prompt: Which of the following functions from R to R is one-one?

options.text: f(x) = x², because each input x gives exactly one output x²

options.diagnosis: Missed that |−a| = |a| pairs two inputs to one output; did not hunt for collisions.
Ignored periodicity: sin 0 = sin π = 0 already breaks injectivity.

question.explanation: f(x) = 2x + 3 is one-one: 2x1 + 3 = 2x2 + 3 forces x1 = x2. x² fails since f(−1) = f(1) = 1 — 'each input has one output' is the definition of a FUNCTION, not of one-one. |x| and sin x also send distinct inputs to equal outputs.

micros.title: Onto (Surjective) Functions
micros.description: Decide whether every element of the codomain is attained: solve f(x) = y for arbitrary y in the codomain, or exhibit a y with no pre-image. Contrast range with codomain.
outcomes: Can prove or disprove surjectivity for functions like f: R→R, f(x) = x² or f(x) = 2x + 3
Can adjust the codomain to make a given function onto

micros.title: Composition of Functions
micros.description: Compute (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)), feeding the output of the inner function into the outer one, and show with examples that g∘f and f∘g generally differ.
outcomes: Can compute g∘f and f∘g for algebraic and trigonometric functions
Can give an example where g∘f ≠ f∘g and explain why order matters

question.prompt: If f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2x + 1, then (g∘f)(x) equals:

options.diagnosis: Attempted g(f(x)) but distributed 2 over x² + x; algebra slip after a correct setup.

question.explanation: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(x²) = 2x² + 1. Computing (f∘g)(x) = (2x+1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1 swaps the order — composition is not commutative — and 2x³ + x² is the PRODUCT g(x)·f(x), which is not composition at all.

micros.title: Invertible Functions and Finding f⁻¹
micros.description: A function has an inverse exactly when it is one-one and onto (bijective). Find f⁻¹ for simple bijections by solving y = f(x) for x, and verify f⁻¹∘f = identity.
outcomes: Can state and apply the bijectivity criterion for invertibility
Can compute f⁻¹ explicitly for functions like f(x) = 3x + 2 or f(x) = (x−1)/(x+2)
Can distinguish f⁻¹(x) from the reciprocal 1/f(x)

question.prompt: The function f: R → R, f(x) = 3x + 2 is invertible. Its inverse f⁻¹(x) is:

options.diagnosis: Reversed only the signs, not the operations; never solved y = 3x + 2 for x.
Undid the operations in the wrong order: added 2 before dividing instead of subtracting first.

question.explanation: Set y = 3x + 2 and solve for x: x = (y − 2)/3, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 2)/3. Check: f⁻¹(f(x)) = ((3x+2) − 2)/3 = x. The reciprocal 1/f(x) is a completely different function — f⁻¹ undoes f, it does not divide 1 by it.

micros.title: Restricting Domain and Codomain to Force Invertibility
micros.description: A non-bijective function becomes invertible after restricting its domain (to make it one-one) and shrinking its codomain to the range (to make it onto), e.g. x² on [0, ∞).
outcomes: Can choose a restricted domain and codomain that make functions like x² or sin x bijective
Can explain why the restriction is necessary before an inverse can exist

micros.title: What sin⁻¹x Means (and Doesn't)
micros.description: sin⁻¹x is the inverse FUNCTION of a restricted sine, not the reciprocal 1/sin x. Because sine is not one-one on R, its domain must be cut down before an inverse can exist.
outcomes: Can explain why sin, cos, tan need restricted domains to be invertible
Can distinguish sin⁻¹x from cosec x = 1/sin x in notation and meaning

question.prompt: Which statement correctly describes sin⁻¹x?

options.text: The angle in [−π/2, π/2] whose sine is x
1/sin x, the reciprocal of sin x

options.diagnosis: Moved the −1 exponent onto the argument; parsing error in function notation.

options.text: Any angle whose sine is x
options.diagnosis: Ignores the principal branch: without restricting to [−π/2, π/2] there are infinitely many such angles and sin⁻¹ would not be a function.

question.explanation: sin⁻¹ is the inverse of the sine function restricted to [−π/2, π/2]: it returns the unique angle in that interval with the given sine. The reciprocal of sin x is written cosec x — the superscript −1 on a function name means inverse function, not power.

micros.title: Principal-value Branches: Domains and Ranges
micros.description: Memorise and justify the principal branches: sin⁻¹: [−1,1] → [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹: [−1,1] → [0, π], tan⁻¹: R → (−π/2, π/2), and why these particular intervals are chosen.
outcomes: Can state domain and range of sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ without error
Can explain why cos⁻¹ needs [0, π] rather than [−π/2, π/2]

micros.title: Evaluating Principal Values
micros.description: Evaluate expressions like sin⁻¹(1/2), cos⁻¹(−1/2), tan⁻¹(−1), landing in the correct principal branch — especially for negative arguments where sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ give negative angles but cos⁻¹ gives an angle in (π/2, π].
outcomes: Can evaluate inverse trig expressions at standard values in the correct branch
Can use sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x and cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x correctly

question.prompt: The principal value of cos⁻¹(−1/2) is:

options.diagnosis: Dropped the negative sign on the argument and evaluated cos⁻¹(1/2).
Confused −1/2 with −√3/2; wrong standard value inside the right branch.

question.explanation: cos⁻¹ takes values in [0, π], never negative. cos⁻¹(−1/2) = π − cos⁻¹(1/2) = π − π/3 = 2π/3, and indeed cos(2π/3) = −1/2. The answer −π/3 uses the sin⁻¹-style branch [−π/2, π/2], which is wrong for cosine.

micros.title: Simplifying sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x)
micros.description: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only when x is inside [−π/2, π/2]; otherwise the answer is the angle in the principal branch with the same sine. Fold arbitrary angles back into the branch using symmetry.
outcomes: Can evaluate sin⁻¹(sin x) and cos⁻¹(cos x) for x outside the principal branch
Can explain why blind cancellation fails using the graph of sin⁻¹(sin x)

question.prompt: sin⁻¹(sin(2π/3)) equals:

options.diagnosis: Folded into the principal branch but flipped the sign; sin(2π/3) is positive so the answer must be positive.
Used sin(2π/3) = 1/2 instead of √3/2; standard-value slip.

question.explanation: sin(2π/3) = sin(π − 2π/3) = sin(π/3) = √3/2. Since 2π/3 lies outside [−π/2, π/2], sin⁻¹ cannot return it: sin⁻¹(√3/2) = π/3. Cancelling sin⁻¹(sin x) to x is only valid inside the principal branch.

micros.title: Identities and Graphs of Inverse Trig Functions
micros.description: Use identities such as sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2, and interpret the graphs of sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹ as reflections of the restricted originals in the line y = x.
outcomes: Can apply sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 to evaluate and simplify expressions
Can sketch inverse trig graphs by reflecting the restricted trig graphs in y = x

micros.title: Matrix Notation, Order and Types
micros.description: A matrix is a rectangular array a_ij with i indexing rows and j columns. Identify order m×n, equality of matrices, and special types: row, column, square, diagonal, scalar, identity, zero.
outcomes: Can state the order of a matrix and locate the entry a_ij
Can classify matrices by type and use equality to solve for unknown entries

micros.title: Matrix Addition and Scalar Multiplication
micros.description: Add matrices of the same order entrywise and multiply a matrix by a scalar; use the algebra of these operations (commutativity, associativity, additive inverse) to solve matrix equations like 2X + A = B.
outcomes: Can add, subtract and scalar-multiply matrices of matching orders
Can solve simple matrix equations for an unknown matrix X

micros.title: Matrix Multiplication: the Row-by-Column Rule
micros.description: Multiply an m×n matrix by an n×p matrix: the (i,j) entry is the dot product of row i with column j. Check compatibility of orders before multiplying — and never multiply entry-by-entry.
outcomes: Can decide when a product AB is defined and state its order
Can compute 2×2 and 3×3 products accurately with the row-by-column rule

question.prompt: Let A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] and B = [[2, 0], [1, 3]] (rows listed). Then AB equals:

options.diagnosis: Row-column slip in the (2,1) entry: computed 3 + 4 instead of 3×2 + 4×1.

question.explanation: AB = [[1·2 + 2·1, 1·0 + 2·3], [3·2 + 4·1, 3·0 + 4·3]] = [[4, 6], [10, 12]]. Multiplying entry-by-entry gives [[2, 0], [3, 12]], which is not matrix multiplication, and [[2, 4], [10, 14]] is BA — order matters.

micros.title: Why AB ≠ BA: Matrix Algebra Identities
micros.description: Matrix multiplication is associative and distributive but NOT commutative. Consequently number-algebra identities mutate: (A+B)² = A² + AB + BA + B², and (A+B)(A−B) = A² − AB + BA − B².
outcomes: Can produce a concrete pair with AB ≠ BA
Can expand (A+B)² and (A+B)(A−B) correctly without merging AB and BA

question.prompt: For square matrices A and B of the same order, (A + B)² always equals:

options.diagnosis: Dropped both cross terms entirely — the 'freshman's dream' carried into matrices.

question.explanation: (A+B)² = (A+B)(A+B) = A² + AB + BA + B² by distributivity. The terms AB and BA cannot be merged into 2AB unless A and B happen to commute, which matrices generally do not.

micros.title: AB = O Without A = O or B = O
micros.description: Unlike numbers, matrices have zero divisors: nonzero matrices can multiply to the zero matrix, and AB = AC does not allow cancelling A. Build and verify explicit examples.
outcomes: Can exhibit nonzero A, B with AB = O
Can explain why cancellation fails and connect it to A not being invertible

question.prompt: A and B are 2×2 matrices with AB = O (the zero matrix). Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is possible that A ≠ O and B ≠ O
Necessarily A = O or B = O
Necessarily both A = O and B = O
options.diagnosis: Even stronger version of the no-zero-divisors belief; also fails for numbers (2 × 0 = 0).

options.text: B must be the inverse of A
options.diagnosis: Confused the zero matrix with the identity: AB = I is the inverse condition, not AB = O.

question.explanation: Take A = [[0, 1], [0, 0]] and B = [[1, 0], [0, 0]]: both are nonzero, yet AB = O. Matrices, unlike real numbers, have zero divisors — so AB = O never justifies concluding a factor is zero.

micros.title: Transpose, Symmetric and Skew-symmetric Matrices
micros.description: Form the transpose by swapping rows and columns; use (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. Classify square matrices as symmetric (Aᵀ = A) or skew-symmetric (Aᵀ = −A), and split any square matrix into a symmetric plus skew-symmetric part.
outcomes: Can compute transposes and apply (A + B)ᵀ, (kA)ᵀ, (AB)ᵀ rules
Can verify symmetry/skew-symmetry and write A = (A + Aᵀ)/2 + (A − Aᵀ)/2

micros.title: Identity Matrix and Invertibility
micros.description: The identity matrix I satisfies AI = IA = A. A square matrix A is invertible when some B gives AB = BA = I; the inverse is unique, and (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹. Verification by direct multiplication.
outcomes: Can verify a proposed inverse by computing AB and BA
Can state and use uniqueness of the inverse and the reversal rule (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹

micros.title: 2×2 Determinants and What They Detect
micros.description: Compute |[[a, b], [c, d]]| = ad − bc, connect a zero determinant to the rows being proportional (singular matrix), and to a pair of linear equations having no unique solution.
outcomes: Can evaluate 2×2 determinants quickly and accurately
Can link |A| = 0 to proportional rows and to non-unique solutions of linear systems

micros.title: Minors and Cofactors
micros.description: The minor M_ij deletes row i and column j and takes the determinant of what remains; the cofactor C_ij = (−1)^(i+j) M_ij attaches the checkerboard sign. Fluency here prevents sign errors in every later computation.
outcomes: Can compute any minor and cofactor of a 3×3 matrix
Can reproduce the (−1)^(i+j) sign checkerboard from the formula rather than memory

question.prompt: For A = [[2, 3, 1], [4, 0, 5], [6, 7, 8]] (rows listed), the cofactor C₁₂ is:

options.diagnosis: Gave the minor M₁₂; forgot the sign factor (−1)^(1+2) = −1.
Computed C₂₁ instead of C₁₂; deleted the wrong row and column.
Added the cross products 4×8 + 5×6 instead of subtracting; determinant rule misremembered.

question.explanation: Delete row 1, column 2: M₁₂ = |[[4, 5], [6, 8]]| = 4×8 − 5×6 = 32 − 30 = 2. Then C₁₂ = (−1)^(1+2) × 2 = −2. The checkerboard sign at position (1,2) is negative.

micros.title: Evaluating 3×3 Determinants by Cofactor Expansion
micros.description: Expand a 3×3 determinant along any row or column as Σ a_ij C_ij, choosing the row or column with the most zeros. Confirm the answer is independent of the row chosen.
outcomes: Can expand along any row or column and get the same value
Can pick the expansion line strategically to minimise arithmetic

micros.title: Properties of Determinants
micros.description: Row swaps flip the sign; a common factor of one row comes out once, so |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix; identical or proportional rows force zero; |AB| = |A||B| but |A + B| ≠ |A| + |B| in general.
outcomes: Can predict the effect of row operations on a determinant
Can apply |kA| = kⁿ|A| and |AB| = |A||B|, and refute |A+B| = |A|+|B| with a counterexample

question.prompt: A is a 3×3 matrix with |A| = 5. The value of |2A| is:

options.diagnosis: Used k⁴ instead of k³; miscounted the number of rows each carrying a factor of 2.

question.explanation: 2A multiplies EVERY row by 2, and each of the 3 rows releases one factor of 2: |2A| = 2³|A| = 8 × 5 = 40. |kA| = k|A| would be true only if just one row were scaled.

micros.title: Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
micros.description: adj A is the transpose of the cofactor matrix; A · adj A = |A| I, so A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| whenever |A| ≠ 0. A matrix with |A| = 0 is singular and has no inverse.
outcomes: Can compute adj A for 2×2 and 3×3 matrices
Can compute A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| and verify AA⁻¹ = I
Can recognise singular matrices as non-invertible

question.prompt: For A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]] (rows listed), A⁻¹ equals:

options.diagnosis: Used |A| = 2 instead of −2; sign slip in ad − bc = 4 − 6.
Formed the adjoint by swapping the diagonal but forgot to negate the off-diagonal entries.

question.explanation: |A| = 1×4 − 2×3 = −2 and adj A = [[4, −2], [−3, 1]] (swap diagonal, negate off-diagonal). So A⁻¹ = adj A / |A| = (−1/2)[[4, −2], [−3, 1]]. Forgetting to divide by |A| gives adj A itself, which fails AA⁻¹ = I.

micros.title: Solving Linear Systems by the Matrix Method
micros.description: Write a system as AX = B and solve X = A⁻¹B when |A| ≠ 0. When |A| = 0, use (adj A)B to distinguish inconsistent systems from ones with infinitely many solutions.
outcomes: Can solve 2- and 3-variable systems via X = A⁻¹B
Can classify a system as unique / inconsistent / infinite using |A| and (adj A)B

micros.title: Continuity at a Point: the Three-part Test
micros.description: f is continuous at a exactly when the left limit, right limit and f(a) all exist AND are equal. Apply the test to piecewise and rational functions, and classify what fails when a function is discontinuous.
outcomes: Can run the three-part continuity test at a point
Can name which ingredient fails (limit missing, value missing, or unequal) in a discontinuity

question.prompt: Define f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = 4. Is f continuous at x = 3?

options.text: No: the limit is 6 but f(3) = 4, and the two must be equal
Yes, because the limit as x → 3 exists
No, because f is not defined at x = 3
options.diagnosis: Did not read the definition: f(3) IS defined (as 4); the failure is the mismatch, not a missing value.

question.explanation: For x ≠ 3, f(x) = (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3) = x + 3, so the limit at 3 is 6. Continuity needs limit = value: 6 ≠ 4, so f is discontinuous at 3. Having a defined value, or an existing limit, is necessary but not sufficient — they must agree.

micros.title: Choosing Parameters for Continuity of Piecewise Functions
micros.description: Given a piecewise function with an unknown constant (e.g. f(x) = kx² for x ≤ 2, f(x) = 3 for x > 2), equate the one-sided limits and the value at the joint to solve for the constant.
outcomes: Can set up and solve the matching equation at the junction point
Can verify the resulting function is continuous by re-running the three-part test

micros.title: Differentiability Implies Continuity — Not Conversely
micros.description: Differentiability at a point requires equal left-hand and right-hand derivatives. Every differentiable function is continuous, but |x| at 0 is continuous with a corner: continuity does not buy smoothness.
outcomes: Can check differentiability by comparing one-sided derivatives
Can state and instantiate the one-way implication with |x| at 0

question.prompt: At x = 0, the function f(x) = |x| is:

options.diagnosis: Reversed the implication: differentiability is the STRONGER condition and always brings continuity with it.
Misread the V-shaped graph as broken; |x| has no jump at 0, only a corner.

question.explanation: |x| → 0 as x → 0 from both sides and |0| = 0, so it is continuous. But the left-hand derivative is −1 while the right-hand derivative is +1; since they differ, f′(0) does not exist. Corners are continuous, not smooth.

micros.title: The Chain Rule for Composite Functions
micros.description: Differentiate f(g(x)) as f′(g(x)) · g′(x): outer derivative evaluated at the inner function, times the inner derivative. Drill on trig, power and nested compositions until the inner factor is never dropped.
outcomes: Can differentiate compositions like sin(x²), (3x² + 1)⁵, cos³x
Can handle double compositions such as sin(cos(x²))

question.prompt: The derivative of sin(x²) with respect to x is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied by the inner derivative but never differentiated the outer sine to cosine.
Differentiated the inner function INSIDE the argument instead of multiplying outside; chain rule structure garbled.

question.explanation: With outer f(u) = sin u and inner u = x²: d/dx sin(x²) = cos(x²) · d/dx(x²) = 2x cos(x²). Stopping at cos(x²) amputates the chain — the inner derivative 2x must multiply the result.

micros.title: Implicit Differentiation and Inverse Trig Derivatives
micros.description: Differentiate relations like x² + y² = 25 term-by-term, attaching dy/dx to every y-derivative via the chain rule, then solve for dy/dx. Derive and use d/dx sin⁻¹x = 1/√(1−x²) and d/dx tan⁻¹x = 1/(1+x²).
outcomes: Can find dy/dx from an implicit relation
Can differentiate expressions containing sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹

micros.title: Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions
micros.description: Use d/dx eˣ = eˣ, d/dx ln x = 1/x, d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a, combined with the chain rule for forms like e^(3x²) and ln(sin x).
outcomes: Can differentiate exponential and logarithmic compositions
Can explain why aˣ needs the extra ln a factor

micros.title: Logarithmic Differentiation
micros.description: For functions of the form u(x)^v(x) or unwieldy products/quotients, take ln of both sides, differentiate implicitly, and multiply back by y. The classic: d/dx xˣ = xˣ(1 + ln x).
outcomes: Can differentiate xˣ and similar variable-power functions
Can decide when logarithmic differentiation is the efficient route

micros.title: Parametric Differentiation and Second Derivatives
micros.description: For x = f(t), y = g(t), compute dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); iterate carefully for d²y/dx² by differentiating dy/dx with respect to t and dividing by dx/dt again. Compute second derivatives of explicit functions.
outcomes: Can compute dy/dx for parametric curves like x = a cos t, y = a sin t
Can compute second derivatives, including the parametric case

micros.title: Derivative as an Instantaneous Rate of Change
micros.description: Interpret dy/dx as the rate of change of y with respect to x in applied units — marginal cost, velocity, rate of area growth with radius — and evaluate rates at specific instants.
outcomes: Can compute and interpret a rate of change with correct units
Can translate 'rate of change of A with respect to r' into dA/dr

micros.title: Related Rates: Differentiating Through Time
micros.description: When two quantities are linked by a geometric relation, differentiate the RELATION with respect to time t using the chain rule, and only then substitute the instant's values. Balloons, ladders, melting cubes.
outcomes: Can set up dA/dt = (dA/dr)(dr/dt)-style chains from a geometric formula
Can explain why substituting values before differentiating destroys the problem

question.prompt: The radius of a circle is increasing at 2 cm/s. How fast is the area increasing when the radius is 5 cm?

options.diagnosis: Reported the AREA πr² at r = 5, not its rate of change; never differentiated.
Computed 2π(dr/dt) — forgot the factor r when differentiating πr².

question.explanation: A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr · dr/dt = 2π(5)(2) = 20π cm²/s. Substituting r = 5 BEFORE differentiating gives A = 25π, a constant whose derivative is 0 — the classic related-rates trap.

micros.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions via the Sign of f′
micros.description: f is increasing where f′ > 0 and decreasing where f′ < 0. Solve the inequality f′(x) > 0, present intervals of monotonicity, and keep the sign of f itself firmly separate from the sign of f′.
outcomes: Can find intervals of increase/decrease by solving f′(x) > 0 and f′(x) < 0
Can articulate why the sign of f says nothing about monotonicity

question.prompt: The function f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 is increasing exactly on:

options.diagnosis: Solved f′(x) < 0 (or flipped the inequality); found the decreasing interval instead.
Differentiated incorrectly to x − 4 (or solved 2x > 4 as x > 4); the correct root of f′(x) = 2x − 4 is x = 2.

question.explanation: f′(x) = 2x − 4 > 0 ⟺ x > 2, so f increases on (2, ∞). Note f(x) = (x−2)² + 1 is positive EVERYWHERE, yet f still decreases on (−∞, 2): positivity of f and increase of f are unrelated properties.

micros.title: Critical Points and the First-derivative Test
micros.description: Find points where f′ = 0 or f′ fails to exist, then classify them by the SIGN CHANGE of f′: + to − gives a local max, − to + a local min, no change (like x³ at 0) gives neither.
outcomes: Can locate critical points and run the first-derivative sign test
Can exhibit a critical point that is not an extremum

question.prompt: For f(x) = x³, we have f′(0) = 0. At x = 0 the function has:

options.text: Neither a local maximum nor a local minimum

options.diagnosis: Confused 'not an extremum' with 'not a critical point': f′(0) = 0 makes x = 0 critical by definition.

question.explanation: f′(x) = 3x² ≥ 0 on both sides of 0 — the sign of f′ does not change, so x³ keeps rising through the origin. f′(c) = 0 is necessary for an interior extremum but never sufficient; the sign change is what decides.

micros.title: The Second-derivative Test
micros.description: At a critical point c with f′(c) = 0: f″(c) < 0 means local max, f″(c) > 0 means local min, and f″(c) = 0 is inconclusive — fall back to the first-derivative test.
outcomes: Can classify critical points using f″
Can recognise the inconclusive case f″(c) = 0 and switch tests

micros.title: Absolute Extrema on a Closed Interval
micros.description: On [a, b], the absolute maximum and minimum occur at critical points OR at the endpoints. Build the candidate list (critical points inside the interval plus both endpoints), evaluate f at each, and compare.
outcomes: Can execute the closed-interval method completely, endpoints included
Can discard critical points that fall outside the interval

question.prompt: The absolute maximum value of f(x) = x³ − 3x on the interval [0, 3] is:

options.diagnosis: Used the critical point x = −1 (where f = 2), which lies OUTSIDE [0, 3].
Evaluated only the left endpoint x = 0; never compared all candidates.

question.explanation: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = ±1; only x = 1 lies in [0, 3]. Candidates: f(0) = 0, f(1) = −2, f(3) = 27 − 9 = 18. The absolute maximum is 18, attained at the ENDPOINT x = 3 — checking only critical points would wrongly return −2.

micros.title: Optimisation Word Problems
micros.description: Translate a story (maximum area, minimum cost, fastest route) into a one-variable function using the constraint, find and classify its critical points, and answer in context with the nature of the optimum verified.
outcomes: Can set up the objective function and eliminate a variable via the constraint
Can verify max/min with a derivative test and state the answer with units

micros.title: The Antiderivative Idea and the Constant of Integration
micros.description: Integration reverses differentiation: F is an antiderivative of f when F′ = f. Because constants die under d/dx, every answer carries + C — a whole family of curves, one for each constant.
outcomes: Can antidifferentiate power functions with the reversed power rule (exponent up, then divide)
Can explain why + C is mandatory and what it represents geometrically

question.prompt: ∫ x² dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Raised the power but forgot to divide by the new exponent 3.

question.explanation: The power rule in reverse: raise the exponent to 3, divide by 3, and add the constant: ∫x² dx = x³/3 + C. Check by differentiating: d/dx(x³/3 + C) = x². Answering 2x differentiates instead of integrating; omitting + C loses infinitely many antiderivatives.

micros.title: The Table of Standard Integrals
micros.description: Command the standard forms: xⁿ, 1/x, eˣ, aˣ, sin x, cos x, sec²x, 1/(1+x²), 1/√(1−x²) — each verified by differentiating the claimed answer, with special care on signs (∫sin x dx = −cos x + C).
outcomes: Can quote and apply the standard integral table accurately, signs included
Can verify any table entry by differentiation

micros.title: Integration by Substitution
micros.description: When the integrand contains a function AND (a constant multiple of) its derivative, set u equal to the inner function so du absorbs the derivative factor: ∫2x cos(x²) dx becomes ∫cos u du.
outcomes: Can spot the u–du pair and carry out the substitution completely
Can convert back to x and verify by differentiating

question.prompt: ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign flipped: confused ∫cos u du = sin u with ∫sin u du = −cos u.
Substituted u = x² but never let du = 2x dx absorb the factor 2; double-counted it.

question.explanation: Let u = x², so du = 2x dx — the 2x in the integrand is exactly du. Then ∫cos u du = sin u + C = sin(x²) + C. Differentiate to confirm: cos(x²)·2x. Multiplying the pieces' separate integrals (x²·sin(x²)) is not a valid rule.

micros.title: Integration by Parts
micros.description: ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du, with u chosen by ILATE (Inverse trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). Handles products like x·eˣ, x·sin x, ln x that substitution cannot touch.
outcomes: Can choose u and dv sensibly and execute the formula
Can handle repeated application and the ∫eˣ(f + f′) shortcut

question.prompt: ∫ x eˣ dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip in the parts formula: used uv + ∫v du instead of uv − ∫v du.
Treated x as a constant that integration ignores; only integrated the eˣ factor.

question.explanation: Take u = x (algebraic before exponential in ILATE), dv = eˣ dx: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ − ∫eˣ dx = x eˣ − eˣ + C. Check: d/dx(xeˣ − eˣ) = eˣ + xeˣ − eˣ = xeˣ. Integrating each factor separately and multiplying — (x²/2)eˣ — is not a valid rule: differentiation of products needs the product rule, so integration of products needs parts.

micros.title: Integration by Partial Fractions
micros.description: Split a proper rational function with factorable denominator into simpler fractions — A/(x−a) + B/(x−b), with repeated-factor and quadratic-factor patterns — then integrate each piece to logarithms and arctangents.
outcomes: Can decompose rational integrands with distinct and repeated linear factors
Can integrate the resulting pieces, e.g. ∫dx/((x−1)(x+2))

micros.title: The Definite Integral as a Limit of Sums
micros.description: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the limit of Riemann sums: slice [a, b] into n strips, sum the strip areas f(xᵢ)·Δx, and let n → ∞. This is what the integral MEANS; the Fundamental Theorem is what makes it computable.
outcomes: Can set up a Riemann sum for a simple function and pass to the limit
Can interpret the definite integral as signed area accumulated from a to b

micros.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
micros.description: If F′ = f on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a): upper-limit value minus lower-limit value, in that order, and no + C. The bridge between antiderivatives and areas.
outcomes: Can evaluate definite integrals via F(b) − F(a) with correct order and signs
Can explain why the constant of integration cancels in definite integrals

question.prompt: ∫₁² 2x dx equals:

options.diagnosis: Evaluated F(2) = 4 only; forgot to subtract the lower-limit value F(1) = 1.

question.explanation: An antiderivative of 2x is x². By the Fundamental Theorem: ∫₁² 2x dx = [x²]₁² = 2² − 1² = 4 − 1 = 3. Subtracting in the wrong order gives −3; adding gives 5. And a definite integral is a NUMBER — no + C appears.

micros.title: Properties of Definite Integrals
micros.description: Exploit structure instead of computing: swapping limits flips the sign, ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx = ∫₀ᵃ f(a−x)dx, splitting at an interior point, and even/odd symmetry on [−a, a] (odd integrands give 0).
outcomes: Can apply the king property f(x) → f(a−x) to evaluate resistant integrals
Can use even/odd symmetry and limit-splitting to shortcut evaluation

micros.title: Sketching the Region Before Integrating
micros.description: Draw the curves, lines and axis limits first: find intercepts and intersection points, decide where each curve sits relative to the axis and to the other curve. The sketch dictates the limits and the integrand.
outcomes: Can sketch regions bounded by a parabola/circle/line combination
Can find intersection points algebraically to serve as integration limits

micros.title: Area Under a Curve Between Two Ordinates
micros.description: For f ≥ 0 on [a, b], the area between the curve, the x-axis and the ordinates x = a, x = b is ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx. Also compute areas against the y-axis via ∫ x dy.
outcomes: Can compute the area under a non-negative curve as a definite integral
Can switch to y-integration when the region is naturally bounded by y-limits

micros.title: Handling Regions Below the Axis
micros.description: The definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative. For true geometric area, split the integral at every axis crossing and add ABSOLUTE values of the pieces — never let lobes cancel.
outcomes: Can locate axis crossings and split the integral there
Can report total geometric area as the sum of absolute lobe areas

question.prompt: The total area enclosed between the curve y = sin x and the x-axis from x = 0 to x = 2π is:

options.diagnosis: Summed absolute lobe sizes but attached a stray negative sign; area can never be negative.

question.explanation: ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = (−(−1)) − (−1) = 2 and ∫_π^{2π} sin x dx = −2. The plain integral over [0, 2π] is 0 because the lobes cancel — but the GEOMETRIC area is |2| + |−2| = 4. Split at the crossing x = π and add absolute values.

micros.title: Area Between Two Curves
micros.description: Find the intersection points, establish which curve is on top over the interval, and integrate (upper − lower). If the curves swap positions, split the integral at the swap point.
outcomes: Can find intersections and identify the upper curve on each sub-interval
Can compute areas like the region between y = x and y = x²

question.prompt: The area of the region enclosed between y = x and y = x² is:

options.diagnosis: Added the two integrals (1/2 + 1/3) instead of subtracting lower from upper.
Integrated only the line y = x over [0, 1]; forgot to remove the region under the parabola.

question.explanation: The curves meet where x = x², i.e. x = 0 and x = 1, and on (0, 1) the line lies above the parabola (at x = 1/2: 0.5 > 0.25). Area = ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = 1/2 − 1/3 = 1/6. Integrating (x² − x) — lower minus upper — produces the impossible negative area.

micros.title: Areas of Standard Regions: Circles, Ellipses, Parabola–Line
micros.description: Assemble the full toolkit on classic board configurations: area of a circle or ellipse by integration (using symmetry and quarter-regions), and mixed regions like a parabola cut by a chord.
outcomes: Can derive the area of a circle x² + y² = a² or ellipse by integrating a quarter and multiplying by 4
Can compute the area between a parabola and a chord line

micros.title: Order and Degree of a Differential Equation
micros.description: Order = highest derivative present; degree = the power of THAT highest derivative once the equation is polynomial in its derivatives (and undefined otherwise). Two different dials — do not cross the wires.
outcomes: Can read off order and degree, including when radicals must first be cleared
Can recognise equations where the degree is not defined

question.prompt: For the differential equation (d²y/dx²)³ + (dy/dx)⁴ + y = 0, the order and degree are respectively:

options.diagnosis: Took the highest power appearing ANYWHERE; degree is the power of the highest-ORDER derivative only.
Read the exponent 4 on dy/dx as an order; order counts differentiation, not powers.

question.explanation: The highest derivative present is d²y/dx² → order 2. The equation is polynomial in derivatives, and that highest derivative carries power 3 → degree 3. The power 4 sits on the lower-order dy/dx and is irrelevant to the degree.

micros.title: Verifying Solutions of Differential Equations
micros.description: Substitute a candidate function into the equation: differentiate it as many times as needed and check the identity holds for all x. Verification builds the meaning of 'solution' before any solving technique.
outcomes: Can verify that a given function satisfies a given differential equation
Can show a candidate FAILS to be a solution by exhibiting the mismatch

micros.title: General vs Particular Solutions
micros.description: The general solution of an order-n equation carries n independent arbitrary constants; initial conditions pin them down to a particular solution. The number of constants matches the ORDER, not the degree.
outcomes: Can distinguish general from particular solutions and count constants correctly
Can apply an initial condition to extract the particular solution

micros.title: Solving Separable Equations
micros.description: Rewrite dy/dx = g(x)h(y) as dy/h(y) = g(x) dx — a multiplicative separation, never additive — integrate both sides, keep ONE arbitrary constant, and simplify it legitimately (e.g. e^C → A).
outcomes: Can separate variables correctly and integrate both sides
Can manage the constant of integration through exponentials and note solutions lost by division

question.prompt: The general solution of dy/dx = 2xy is:

options.diagnosis: Integrated the right side with respect to x while treating y as a constant — the variables were never separated.
Integrated 2x incorrectly as 2x again; ∫2x dx = x², not 2x.

question.explanation: Separate: dy/y = 2x dx. Integrate: ln|y| = x² + C₁, so y = ±e^(C₁) e^(x²) = C e^(x²). Dropping the constant gives only ONE solution curve out of infinitely many; the constant must ride along from the moment of integration.

micros.title: First-order Linear Equations and the Integrating Factor
micros.description: For dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x), multiply through by IF = e^(∫P dx) — integrate P FIRST, then exponentiate — so the left side collapses to d/dx(y·IF); then y·IF = ∫Q·IF dx + C.
outcomes: Can compute the integrating factor correctly
Can solve equations like dy/dx + y/x = x² end to end

question.prompt: The integrating factor of the differential equation dy/dx + (1/x)y = x², for x > 0, is:

options.diagnosis: Used P(x) itself as the integrating factor; skipped both the integration and the exponentiation.

question.explanation: IF = e^(∫P dx) = e^(∫dx/x) = e^(ln x) = x (for x > 0). Both steps are essential: integrate P to get ln x, THEN exponentiate. Multiplying the equation by x gives d/dx(xy) = x³, which integrates immediately.

micros.title: Modelling with Differential Equations: Growth and Decay
micros.description: dy/dt = ky yields y = y₀e^(kt): exponential growth (k > 0) or decay (k < 0). Fit k and y₀ from data, and answer doubling-time / half-life style questions for populations, investments and radioactivity.
outcomes: Can derive y = y₀e^(kt) from dy/dt = ky with an initial condition
Can solve applied growth/decay problems including doubling time

micros.title: Vectors in Component Form: Magnitude and Unit Vectors
micros.description: Write vectors as xi + yj + zk, compute magnitude |a| = √(x² + y² + z²), build the unit vector a/|a|, and distinguish vectors (magnitude + direction) from scalars.
outcomes: Can compute magnitudes and unit vectors in 3D
Can identify equal, collinear and coinitial vectors from components

micros.title: Vector Addition and the Section Formula
micros.description: Add vectors componentwise (triangle/parallelogram law) — magnitudes do NOT simply add unless the vectors are parallel. Use the section formula (mb + na)/(m + n) for points dividing a segment.
outcomes: Can add and subtract vectors and interpret the triangle law geometrically
Can find position vectors of internal/external division points

question.prompt: Vectors a and b are perpendicular with |a| = 3 and |b| = 4. Then |a + b| equals:

options.diagnosis: Subtracted the magnitudes; that bounds |a − b| for parallel vectors, not this sum.
Multiplied the magnitudes — confused vector addition with some product.

question.explanation: |a + b|² = |a|² + |b|² + 2a·b = 9 + 16 + 0 = 25, so |a + b| = 5 — the Pythagorean diagonal of the rectangle with sides 3 and 4. Magnitudes add to 7 only when the vectors point the SAME way; direction always matters.

micros.title: The Dot Product: a Scalar from Two Vectors
micros.description: a·b = |a||b|cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃ — the output is a NUMBER. Use it to find the angle between vectors; it is commutative and distributes over addition.
outcomes: Can compute dot products in component form
Can extract cos θ = a·b/(|a||b|) and interpret its sign

question.prompt: If a = 2i + 3j − k and b = i − j + 2k, then a·b equals:

options.diagnosis: Sign slip: computed 2 + 3 − 2 by ignoring the negative components.
Dropped the third term (−1)(2) = −2 from the sum; incomplete expansion.

question.explanation: a·b = (2)(1) + (3)(−1) + (−1)(2) = 2 − 3 − 2 = −3. The dot product is a SCALAR — multiplying matching components and summing collapses everything to a single number; 2i − 3j − 2k keeps the terms as a vector, which is a type error.

micros.title: Projection of One Vector on Another
micros.description: The scalar projection of a on b is a·b/|b|, the vector projection is (a·b/|b|²)b. Interpret as the shadow of a along b's direction.
outcomes: Can compute scalar and vector projections
Can explain the difference between the two and when each is asked for

micros.title: Perpendicularity and the Zero Dot Product
micros.description: For nonzero vectors, a·b = 0 means a ⊥ b — not that either vector vanishes. Use this test to find unknowns making vectors perpendicular and to verify orthogonality of i, j, k.
outcomes: Can test and impose perpendicularity via a·b = 0
Can state the correct logic: a·b = 0 ⟹ a = 0 or b = 0 or a ⊥ b

question.prompt: a and b are NONZERO vectors with a·b = 0. What can you conclude?

options.diagnosis: Swapped the tests: parallel vectors give a×b = 0; parallel NONZERO vectors have a·b = ±|a||b| ≠ 0.
Invented a magnitude condition; the dot product vanishing constrains the ANGLE (cos θ = 0), not the lengths.

question.explanation: a·b = |a||b|cos θ. With both magnitudes nonzero, the product can only vanish through cos θ = 0, i.e. θ = 90°. Unlike real-number multiplication, a zero dot product does not force a zero factor — perpendicularity is the third way.

micros.title: The Cross Product via the Determinant Rule
micros.description: a×b = |i j k; a₁ a₂ a₃; b₁ b₂ b₃| — the output is a VECTOR perpendicular to both, with |a×b| = |a||b|sin θ. It is anti-commutative: a×b = −(b×a).
outcomes: Can compute cross products with the determinant expansion
Can state and use a×b = −(b×a) and check the result is perpendicular to both inputs

question.prompt: If a × b = 3i − j + 2k, then b × a equals:

options.diagnosis: Confused anti-commutativity with the products cancelling; b × a is the opposite VECTOR, not zero.

question.explanation: The cross product is anti-commutative: b × a = −(a × b) = −3i + j − 2k. Swapping two rows of the defining determinant flips its sign. And the output is a vector — √14 is merely the common MAGNITUDE of both products.

micros.title: Applications of the Cross Product: Areas and Parallelism
micros.description: |a×b| is the area of the parallelogram on a and b (half it for the triangle); a×b = 0 for nonzero vectors means they are parallel. Compute areas of triangles from vertex coordinates.
outcomes: Can compute parallelogram and triangle areas via cross products
Can test collinearity/parallelism with a×b = 0

micros.title: Direction Ratios and Direction Cosines
micros.description: Direction ratios a, b, c fix a line's direction up to scale; direction cosines l, m, n are the ratios NORMALISED by √(a² + b² + c²), so that l² + m² + n² = 1 always.
outcomes: Can convert direction ratios to direction cosines by dividing by the magnitude
Can verify l² + m² + n² = 1 and recover the angle each axis makes

question.prompt: A line has direction ratios 2, −3, 6. Its direction cosines are:

options.diagnosis: Divided by the sum of absolute values 2 + 3 + 6 = 11 instead of the root-sum-of-squares.
Reported the squared cosines (which sum to 1) instead of the cosines themselves.

question.explanation: The magnitude is √(2² + (−3)² + 6²) = √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7, so (l, m, n) = (2/7, −3/7, 6/7). Check: 4/49 + 9/49 + 36/49 = 1. Raw ratios are only proportional to the cosines — they must be normalised.

micros.title: Equations of a Line in Space
micros.description: Write a line through point a with direction b as r = a + λb, and in Cartesian symmetric form (x−x₁)/a = (y−y₁)/b = (z−z₁)/c; also through two given points. Convert fluently between the two forms.
outcomes: Can write vector and Cartesian equations of lines from point + direction or two points
Can translate between the vector and symmetric forms

micros.title: Angle Between Two Lines; Parallel and Perpendicular Tests
micros.description: cos θ = |b₁·b₂|/(|b₁||b₂|) from the direction vectors. Lines are parallel when direction ratios are proportional and perpendicular when a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0 — keep the two tests straight.
outcomes: Can compute the angle between lines from direction ratios
Can apply the proportionality test for parallel and the zero-dot-product test for perpendicular

question.prompt: Two lines have direction ratios (1, 2, 2) and (2, 1, −2). The lines are:

options.diagnosis: Computed cos θ with a wrong dot product or magnitudes; the dot product here is exactly 0.
Coincidence requires proportional ratios AND a shared point; neither condition holds.

question.explanation: Dot product of directions: (1)(2) + (2)(1) + (2)(−2) = 2 + 2 − 4 = 0, so the lines are perpendicular. Parallelism would need proportional ratios (1/2 = 2/1 = 2/−2 fails immediately).

micros.title: Shortest Distance Between Skew Lines
micros.description: Skew lines neither meet nor run parallel. The shortest distance is |(a₂ − a₁)·(b₁×b₂)|/|b₁×b₂| — the projection of the connecting vector onto the common perpendicular direction b₁×b₂.
outcomes: Can classify a pair of lines as intersecting, parallel or skew
Can compute the shortest distance between skew lines with the formula

micros.title: Equations of a Plane
micros.description: A plane is fixed by its normal n: r·n = d (normal form) or ax + by + cz + d = 0 in Cartesian form, where (a, b, c) are the normal's direction ratios. Build plane equations from a point and normal, or three points.
outcomes: Can write a plane's equation from point + normal and read off the normal from ax + by + cz + d = 0
Can test whether points lie on, or lines lie in, a given plane

micros.title: Angle Between a Line and a Plane
micros.description: The line's direction meets the plane's NORMAL at some angle θ; the angle with the plane itself is the complement 90° − θ, computed via sin φ = |b·n|/(|b||n|). Parallel/perpendicular tests follow from the normal.
outcomes: Can compute the angle between a line and a plane via the normal
Can state why the line–normal and line–plane angles are complementary

question.prompt: A line makes an angle of 30° with the normal to a plane. The angle between the line and the plane is:

options.diagnosis: Treated 'angle with the plane' as always a right angle; only a line ALONG the normal is perpendicular to the plane.
Subtracted from 180° instead of 90°; used supplement instead of complement.

question.explanation: The angle with the plane and the angle with its normal always add to 90°: the plane lies at right angles to the normal. So the required angle is 90° − 30° = 60°. Reporting 30° hands in the line–normal angle by mistake.

micros.title: Distance from a Point to a Plane
micros.description: Distance from (x₁, y₁, z₁) to ax + by + cz + d = 0 is |ax₁ + by₁ + cz₁ + d| / √(a² + b² + c²) — the division by |n| is what converts the raw substitution into a genuine length.
outcomes: Can compute point-to-plane distances with correct normalisation
Can find the distance between parallel planes via a point on one of them

question.prompt: The distance from the point (1, 1, 1) to the plane x + 2y + 2z − 3 = 0 is:

options.diagnosis: Divided by |n|² = 9 instead of |n| = 3; squared the normaliser.
Substituted +3 instead of −3 for the constant term; sign of d mishandled.

question.explanation: Numerator: |1 + 2(1) + 2(1) − 3| = |2| = 2. Normal magnitude: √(1² + 2² + 2²) = √9 = 3. Distance = 2/3. Skipping the division by |n| leaves the un-normalised value 2, which has no geometric meaning as a length.

micros.title: Formulating a Linear Programming Problem
micros.description: Extract decision variables from the story, write the linear objective function Z to maximise or minimise, and translate every resource limit and requirement into a linear constraint — including x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
outcomes: Can define variables and write the objective function from a word problem
Can list ALL constraints including non-negativity

micros.title: Graphing Constraints and the Feasible Region
micros.description: Plot each constraint line, shade the correct half-plane (test with the origin), and intersect all shaded regions with the first quadrant to obtain the feasible region — the set of all allowed decisions.
outcomes: Can shade the correct side of each constraint using a test point
Can identify the feasible region and its vertices from the graph

question.prompt: Which point lies in the feasible region determined by x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0?

options.diagnosis: Checked only the non-negativity conditions; 3 + 2 = 5 violates x + y ≤ 4.
Satisfies neither x + y ≤ 4 nor y ≥ 0; substitution never performed.

question.explanation: (1, 2): 1 + 2 = 3 ≤ 4 ✓, 1 ≥ 0 ✓, 2 ≥ 0 ✓ — all three constraints hold. (−1, 3) satisfies x + y ≤ 4 but breaks x ≥ 0: the non-negativity constraints are real constraints and must be checked every time.

micros.title: The Corner-point Method
micros.description: For a bounded feasible region, the optimum of a linear objective occurs at a VERTEX: find all corner points (intersections that actually lie in the region), evaluate Z at each, and pick the best.
outcomes: Can find corner points by solving pairs of boundary equations and discarding infeasible intersections
Can evaluate Z at every vertex and identify maximum and minimum

question.prompt: The corner points of a bounded feasible region are (0, 0), (5, 0), (3, 4) and (0, 6). The maximum of Z = 4x + y over the region is:

options.diagnosis: Evaluated Z at only some vertices, or assumed the 'highest-looking' corner wins without comparing all four values.
Picked the vertex with the largest coordinate instead of the largest Z; Z weights x four times y here.

question.explanation: Z at the corners: (0,0) → 0, (5,0) → 20, (3,4) → 16, (0,6) → 6. The maximum is 20 at (5, 0). A linear objective over a convex polygon always peaks at a vertex — interior points like (2, 2) with Z = 10 can never beat the best corner.

micros.title: Optima on Unbounded Feasible Regions
micros.description: With an unbounded region the corner-point value is only a CANDIDATE: the optimum exists iff the open half-plane beyond it (Z > M for max, Z < m for min) shares no point with the region. Run this check every time.
outcomes: Can perform the open half-plane test on an unbounded region
Can decide whether a candidate optimum is genuine or the problem has no optimum

question.prompt: Minimising Z = x + 2y over an UNBOUNDED feasible region, the smallest corner-point value is 6. What must you do before declaring 6 the minimum?

options.text: Check whether the open half-plane x + 2y < 6 has any point in common with the feasible region; 6 is the minimum only if it has none
Nothing — the smallest corner value is always the minimum
Conclude no minimum exists, since unbounded regions never have optima
Evaluate Z at a few interior points to see if anything smaller appears

question.explanation: On an unbounded region the region may stretch into territory where Z keeps decreasing forever. The definitive test: intersect the region with the OPEN half-plane x + 2y < 6. Empty intersection → 6 is the true minimum; non-empty → no minimum exists. Unbounded regions sometimes do and sometimes don't have optima — only the test decides.

micros.title: Applied LPP: Diet, Manufacturing and Transport
micros.description: Solve complete board-style problems end to end: formulate from the story, graph, run the corner-point method, and interpret the optimal vertex as a real decision (units to produce, packets to buy).
outcomes: Can solve a full two-variable LPP word problem from text to interpreted answer
Can sanity-check the answer against the constraints and context

micros.title: Conditional Probability from the Definition
micros.description: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) re-scales probability to the world where B has happened. Compute it from given probabilities and from two-way tables, and keep P(A|B) firmly distinct from P(B|A).
outcomes: Can compute conditional probabilities from the definition and from tables
Can explain with an example why P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) in general

question.prompt: Given P(A) = 0.8, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A∩B) = 0.2, the value of P(A|B) is:

options.diagnosis: Multiplied P(A∩B) by P(B) instead of dividing; formula inverted.
Added 0.2 + 0.5; no conditional structure used at all.

question.explanation: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B) = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4. Dividing by P(A) instead gives P(B|A) = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25 — the swapped conditional. The event AFTER the bar supplies the denominator.

micros.title: The Multiplication Rule for Dependent Events
micros.description: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B|A): the second factor must be CONDITIONED on the first event having happened. Essential for without-replacement draws, where the sample space shrinks between picks.
outcomes: Can chain conditional probabilities for sequential draws without replacement
Can decide when the second factor needs updating and when it does not

question.prompt: Two cards are drawn from a standard 52-card pack WITHOUT replacement. The probability that both are kings is:

options.diagnosis: Updated the denominator to 51 but kept 4 kings for the second draw; forgot one king left the pack.
Added 4/52 + 4/52; used the addition rule where the multiplication rule belongs.

question.explanation: P(K₁∩K₂) = P(K₁)·P(K₂|K₁) = (4/52)(3/51) = (1/13)(1/17) = 1/221. After the first king leaves, only 3 kings remain among 51 cards. Squaring 4/52 (= 1/169) pretends the draws are independent, which without replacement they are not.

micros.title: Independent Events vs Mutually Exclusive Events
micros.description: A and B are independent when P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) — knowing one occurred doesn't change the other's probability. Mutually exclusive events CANNOT co-occur, and (for positive-probability events) are never independent.
outcomes: Can test independence numerically with P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B)
Can articulate the difference between independent and mutually exclusive with examples

question.prompt: A and B are INDEPENDENT events with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. Then P(A∩B) equals:

options.text: 0, because independent events cannot occur together

options.diagnosis: Added the probabilities — that computes P(A∪B) for mutually exclusive events, not P(A∩B) for independent ones.
Took min(P(A), P(B)) or assumed B ⊂ A; no multiplication performed.

question.explanation: Independence MEANS P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2. It is mutually EXCLUSIVE events that cannot co-occur (P(A∩B) = 0). Independent events with positive probabilities always can — one happening simply tells you nothing about the other.

micros.title: The Theorem of Total Probability
micros.description: When events E₁, ..., Eₙ partition the sample space, P(A) = Σ P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ): the overall probability of A is the prior-weighted average over the scenarios. Tree diagrams make the sum visible.
outcomes: Can compute P(A) across a partition using a tree diagram
Can verify the partition is genuine (exhaustive and mutually exclusive) before applying the theorem

micros.title: Bayes' Theorem: Reversing the Conditional
micros.description: P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) / Σ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ): update a prior in the light of evidence. The denominator is the total probability of the evidence; the prior must never be ignored, however accurate the 'test'.
outcomes: Can set up the Bayes numerator and total-probability denominator correctly
Can explain base-rate neglect with a rare-disease example

question.prompt: A disease affects 1% of a population. A test detects it with probability 0.9 in the diseased, but also gives a false positive with probability 0.1 in the healthy. A randomly chosen person tests positive. The probability they actually have the disease is:

options.diagnosis: Reported the joint probability P(disease AND positive); never divided by the total probability of testing positive.
Reported the denominator P(positive) itself as the answer; Bayes fraction left unassembled.

question.explanation: P(D|+) = P(D)P(+|D) / [P(D)P(+|D) + P(D′)P(+|D′)] = (0.01)(0.9) / [(0.01)(0.9) + (0.99)(0.1)] = 0.009/0.108 = 1/12 ≈ 0.083. Despite the '90% accurate' test, the disease is so rare that most positives are false — ignoring the 1% base rate inflates the answer tenfold.

micros.title: Discrete Random Variables and Probability Distributions
micros.description: A random variable assigns a number to each outcome; its probability distribution lists each value with its probability, all probabilities non-negative and summing to 1. Build distributions for coin, die and card experiments.
outcomes: Can construct the distribution table of a discrete random variable
Can use Σpᵢ = 1 to find an unknown probability in a table

micros.title: Mean (Expected Value) of a Random Variable
micros.description: E(X) = Σ xᵢpᵢ: the probability-weighted average of the values — the long-run average per trial, not the most likely single outcome. Compute and interpret means of small discrete distributions.
outcomes: Can compute E(X) from a distribution table
Can interpret the mean as a long-run average, including non-attainable values like 3.5 for a die

question.prompt: A random variable X takes values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.3, 0.5, 0.2 respectively. The mean E(X) is:

options.diagnosis: Averaged the values (0 + 1 + 2)/3, ignoring the probabilities entirely.
Summed the values of X; probabilities never entered the computation.
Reported the largest probability instead of the weighted average of the values.

question.explanation: E(X) = Σxᵢpᵢ = 0(0.3) + 1(0.5) + 2(0.2) = 0 + 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. Each value is weighted by how often it occurs; the unweighted average (0+1+2)/3 = 1 would only be right if all three values were equally likely.
